title: The Safehouse of Vienna
premise: Cyrus Dunmore has spent a decade as the invisible fixer-interpreter for Vienna's deniable operations, living above a safe house that officially does not exist. When a real-estate listing surfaces with interior photos — including her own handwriting on the kitchen chalkboard — she realizes someone is flushing her out, and the buyer's shell company traces to the man whose war-crimes testimony she once buried to save a delegation. Racing through Vienna's back channels with a burned analyst and a teenage witness who has become her unlikely family, Cyrus must decide whether to sell the recording that could destroy them all or detonate it publicly before Frankfurt's markets open at 9:00 a.m. She chooses exposure over survival: the secret goes live, the safe house burns, and Cyrus finally steps into the light — alive, disavowed, and no longer alone.
about_author: A. M. Thornbury is the pen name of a former conference interpreter who spent fifteen years working behind closed doors in European diplomacy before turning to fiction. Thornbury writes from a small flat near the Danube Canal and refuses all interviews conducted on the record.

chapters.title: The Listing
chapters.summary: Cyrus Dunmore, POV. Scrolling property listings at 2 a.m., Cyrus finds her safe house for sale — twelve interior photos, her chalkboard notes legible in one. The emotional beat is cold dread: invisibility was her entire architecture of safety, and it has just been punctured by a stranger who knows exactly what those notes mean.

chapters.title: Nine Languages, No Name
chapters.summary: Cyrus, POV. Flashback-woven chapter establishing her role as the delegation's unattributed interpreter and cleaner; she works a routine extraction while mentally cataloguing who could have photographed the house. Beat: competence masking rising paranoia as she realizes the listing used an old photo — pre-renovation, from someone inside her circle.

chapters.title: The Buyer Is a Lie
chapters.summary: Cyrus, POV. She traces the listing's shell company through a notary contact and finds it loops back to Voss Holdings — the family firm of Anton Voss, the arms broker whose testimony she buried years ago. Beat: the past arriving with paperwork; guilt sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Marta Knows the Building
chapters.summary: Marta Ilves, POV — a burned financial analyst hiding in the safe house's basement flat. Marta admits she let a 'building surveyor' in three weeks ago, believing he was sent by their handler. Beat: betrayal within the found family, and forgiveness offered anyway because there is no one else.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Counts Cars
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV — a sixteen-year-old witness under unofficial protection, autistic, who memorizes license plates. He reports a grey Audi circling the block for six days. Beat: tenderness and threat braided together; Tomas sees everything but doesn't yet understand what his seeing will cost.

chapters.title: Handler Ghosted
chapters.summary: Cyrus, POV. Her handler, Kessler, misses two dead-drops; his office is stripped overnight. She realizes the network that protected her is being dismantled from above — someone with ministerial reach. Beat: abandonment; the state she served has quietly deleted her.

chapters.title: What the Tape Holds
chapters.summary: Cyrus, POV. In a bank box she retrieves the recording she never destroyed: Voss ordering the massacre his testimony would have covered, with her own voice interpreting — proof of both his crime and her complicity. Beat: self-confrontation; the secret worth killing for is also the thing that damns her.

chapters.title: An Offer in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: Voss, POV. A rare antagonist chapter: Voss explains, over coffee in a crowded café where nothing can be said aloud, that he wants the tape, offers her money and a new life, and mentions Tomas's school schedule. Beat: velvet menace; the reader understands the stakes are now the boy.

chapters.title: Running the Ring
chapters.summary: Cyrus, Marta, and Tomas, alternating POV. The trio abandons the safe house and moves through Vienna's U-Bahn and flea markets using tradecraft Cyrus learned watching others die. Beat: fugitive intimacy — the found family forged in motion, small jokes between sirens.

chapters.title: The Notary's Ledger
chapters.summary: Cyrus, POV. She blackmails the notary into revealing Voss Holdings' other properties and finds a pattern: every site connects to the failed peace delegation's finances. Beat: revelation — the listing wasn't about her alone; Voss is erasing the delegation's paper trail before an EU audit.

chapters.title: Kessler, Alive and Sorry
chapters.summary: Kessler, POV. The handler resurfaces, half-broken, confessing he traded Cyrus's location for his pension and now wants to help. Beat: unreliable redemption; Cyrus must decide whether forgiveness is strategy or weakness, and chooses both.

chapters.title: Safe House on Fire
chapters.summary: Marta, POV. Voss's men torch the empty safe house; Marta, returning for her mother's letters, barely escapes and is hospitalized under a false name. Beat: grief and rage; the physical home is gone, forcing the question of what 'safe' ever meant.

chapters.title: Hospital Watch
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV. Tomas keeps vigil at Marta's bedside and spots the grey Audi's driver posing as an orderly. Instead of running, he photographs him — his counting habit becoming evidence. Beat: courage from the least protected character; the hunted begin hunting back.

chapters.title: Frankfurt Countdown
chapters.summary: Cyrus, POV. Kessler reveals Voss plans to launder the delegation's missing funds through Frankfurt markets opening Monday 9:00 a.m.; the tape, made public before then, freezes the transaction. Beat: the clock starts ticking — justice and finance bound to the same deadline.

chapters.title: The Journalist Nobody Trusts
chapters.summary: Cyrus, POV. She approaches Lena Brandt, a disgraced investigative reporter, offering the tape if Lena agrees to publish simultaneously across three outlets so it can't be suppressed. Beat: uneasy alliance; trust extended as a calculated gamble that becomes something realer.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Donaukanal
chapters.summary: Kessler, POV. Cornered by Voss's people, Kessler gives up the handoff location — then shoots himself rather than confirm more. Beat: tragedy; the man who sold her twice dies paying a third debt, leaving Cyrus the drop point and a warning note.

chapters.title: Trap at the Handoff
chapters.summary: Cyrus and Tomas, POV. At the Prater handoff, Cyrus walks into Voss's ambush carrying a decoy drive while Tomas, hidden, livestreams the confrontation. Beat: terror and audacity; Cyrus is captured, but the capture itself is being witnessed.

chapters.title: Interrogation, Interpreted
chapters.summary: Cyrus, POV. Voss interrogates her personally; she uses her interpreter's skills to stall, mislead, and record his admissions on the decoy's hidden second channel. Beat: her profession weaponized — language as armor, silence as a blade.

chapters.title: Eight Fifty-One
chapters.summary: Lena and Marta, POV. With Cyrus missing, Lena races to publish and Marta decrypts the decoy's second channel remotely. At 8:51 a.m., the recording hits three newsrooms. Beat: desperate coordination; the found family executes the plan without its center.

chapters.title: Markets Open
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs, minute-by-minute. As Frankfurt opens, the tape goes public; Voss's accounts freeze mid-transfer, his arrest warrant already drafted by a prosecutor who owed Kessler. Beat: cathartic collapse of the powerful; justice arrives not through courts first, but through daylight.

chapters.title: What Cyrus Buried
chapters.summary: Cyrus, POV. Freed in the chaos, Cyrus surrenders voluntarily, giving full testimony including her own complicity, accepting charges to legitimize the case against Voss. Beat: moral climax; she trades freedom for truth, ending the decade of invisibility on her own terms.

chapters.title: A Room with Windows
chapters.summary: Cyrus, Marta, and Tomas, POV epilogue. Months later, awaiting sentencing under protective custody, Cyrus rents a small apartment with big windows — the opposite of a safe house. Marta visits with pastries; Tomas counts trams from the balcony. Beat: quiet resolution; home rebuilt not as concealment but as chosen, visible belonging.
